questions.stem: From the words lettered A to D, choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters underlined: s**ea**t
questions.explanation: Seat has the long pure vowel /iː/. Beat shares that sound. Sit has the short vowel /i/, which is a different phoneme, not a shorter version of the same one. Length is part of the identity of the vowel.

distractorRationale.a: Sit is /i/, the classic short partner of /iː/, and the most common trap
distractorRationale.b: Set has /e/, a different short vowel
distractorRationale.d: Looks like seat plus a letter; it is not a standard word and does not help

questions.stem: Which word has the same vowel sound as sit?
questions.explanation: Sit has short /i/. The first vowel of women is also /i/, despite the letter o. Machine, receive and people all have long /iː/. Matching the letter i in sit to the letter i in machine is the spelling trap this item is built on.

distractorRationale.a: Machine has /iː/, as in seat, not sit
distractorRationale.c: Receive has /iː/ in the second syllable
distractorRationale.d: People has /iː/, another long-vowel spelling of the seat family

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem: From the words lettered A to D, choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter underlined: c**u**t
questions.explanation: Cut has the short vowel /ʌ/. Blood is pronounced /blʌd/, so it matches. The letter u in put is /ʊ/, the o in cot is /ɒ/, and court has long /ɔː/. Same letter, four different vowels.

distractorRationale.a: Put has /ʊ/, as in book, not /ʌ/
distractorRationale.c: Cot has /ɒ/; merging /ʌ/ and /ɒ/ is a common Nigerian-English confusion
distractorRationale.d: Court has /ɔː/, the long vowel of caught

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem: Which word has the same vowel sound as the underlined letters in f**a**ther?
questions.explanation: Father has long /ɑː/. Heart is /hɑːt/, so it shares the sound. Cat and hat have short /æ/, which looks similar on the page because of the letter a but is a different vowel. Examiners use this pair every year.

distractorRationale.a: Cat is /æ/, the short front vowel, not /ɑː/
distractorRationale.b: Hat is also /æ/; doubling the trap does not make it correct

questions.explanation: Boy has /ɔɪ/, a closing diphthong: the tongue glides from an /ɔ/-like start toward /i/ inside one syllable. Seat /iː/, sit /i/ and bird /ɜː/ are pure vowels; the tongue does not glide.

distractorRationale.a: Seat is a long pure vowel /iː/, not a glide
distractorRationale.b: Sit is a short pure vowel /i/
distractorRationale.d: Bird is the long pure vowel /ɜː/

questions.stem: From the words lettered A to D, choose the word that has the same vowel sound as g**o**
questions.explanation: Go has the diphthong /əʊ/. Though is /ðəʊ/, so it matches. Through is /θruː/ (/uː/), thought is /θɔːt/ (/ɔː/), and tough is /tʌf/ (/ʌ/). The shared -ough spelling is irrelevant.

distractorRationale.a: Through has long /uː/, as in food
distractorRationale.c: Thought has long /ɔː/, as in caught
distractorRationale.d: Tough has short /ʌ/, as in cut

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem: From the words lettered A to D, choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters underlined: gr**ea**t
questions.explanation: Great has the diphthong /eɪ/, the same sound as day and they. Break shares /eɪ/. Greet has /iː/; threat and head have the short vowel /e/. The letters ea are among the least reliable spellings in English.

distractorRationale.a: Greet is /iː/; candidates pick it because great and greet look like a pair
distractorRationale.d: Head has /e/, another ea spelling that is not /eɪ/

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem: Which set groups three words that all share the same vowel sound?
questions.explanation: Here, fierce and beard all have the centring diphthong /ɪə/. Sit is /i/ while seat and machine are /iː/; put is /ʊ/ while pool and food are /uː/; though /əʊ/, through /uː/ and thought /ɔː/ are three different vowels.

distractorRationale.d: Three -ough words with three different vowels — the classic spelling trap
